lessons.title: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table
lessons.description: How atoms are built from protons, neutrons and electrons, and what isotopes are.
lessons.content_html:
Inside the Atom

Everything around you is made from tiny particles called atoms. They are incredibly small — a typical atom has a radius of about \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. Despite their tiny size, atoms have a definite internal structure that determines how each element behaves.

At the centre of every atom sits a nucleus. The nucleus is extremely small compared to the overall atom — roughly 1/10,000 of the atom’s diameter — yet it contains nearly all of the atom’s mass. Around the nucleus, electrons move rapidly in regions called energy levels or shells.

Key Fact

The nucleus contains protons (relative charge +1, relative mass 1) and neutrons (relative charge 0, relative mass 1). Electrons (relative charge −1, relative mass nearly zero) orbit the nucleus in shells. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the charges cancel out.

Subatomic Particles

Atoms contain three types of subatomic particles. Protons carry a positive charge and have a relative mass of 1. Neutrons have no charge and also have a relative mass of 1. Electrons carry a negative charge but have a negligible mass — roughly \(\frac{1}{1836}\) of a proton’s mass.

Because protons and electrons carry equal but opposite charges, a neutral atom always contains the same number of each. If an atom has 8 protons, it also has 8 electrons. This balance makes every atom electrically neutral.

In the early 1800s, John Dalton proposed that atoms were solid, indivisible spheres. In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and suggested the plum pudding model — a ball of positive charge with negative electrons scattered through it. Then, in 1909–1911, Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment showed that most of an atom is empty space, with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre. Niels Bohr refined the model in 1913 by placing electrons in fixed energy levels. Finally, James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, completing the modern picture of the atom.

Atomic Number and Mass Number

Every element has a unique atomic number — the number of protons in its nucleus. No two different elements share the same atomic number. On the periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.

The mass number is the total count of protons plus neutrons. To find the number of neutrons, subtract the atomic number from the mass number:

$$\text{neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{atomic number}$$

lessons.title: Electronic Configuration & Trends in the Periodic Table
lessons.description: How the periodic table is organised and electronic configuration links to groups.
lessons.content_html:
The Modern Periodic Table

In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number (the number of protons). This ordering was established after the work of Henry Moseley in 1913, replacing Dmitri Mendeleev’s original arrangement by atomic mass.

The table is organised into horizontal rows called periods and vertical columns called groups. There are seven periods and eight main groups (Groups 1–7 and Group 0). Elements in the same group share similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.

Key Fact

The group number (for Groups 1–7) equals the number of electrons in the outer shell. The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells. For example, potassium (2, 8, 8, 1) is in Group 1 (one outer electron) and Period 4 (four shells).

Electronic Configuration

Electronic configuration describes how electrons are distributed across the energy levels of an atom. Electrons always fill the lowest available energy level first. The first shell can hold a maximum of 2 electrons, while the second and third shells each hold up to 8.

To work out the electronic configuration of any element in the first 20, start with its atomic number (which equals its total number of electrons) and fill the shells in order. For example, magnesium has atomic number 12, so its configuration is 2, 8, 2 — two electrons in the first shell, eight in the second, and two in the third.

Hydrogen (1): 1. Helium (2): 2. Lithium (3): 2, 1. Beryllium (4): 2, 2. Boron (5): 2, 3. Carbon (6): 2, 4. Nitrogen (7): 2, 5. Oxygen (8): 2, 6. Fluorine (9): 2, 7. Neon (10): 2, 8. Sodium (11): 2, 8, 1. Magnesium (12): 2, 8, 2. Aluminium (13): 2, 8, 3. Silicon (14): 2, 8, 4. Phosphorus (15): 2, 8, 5. Sulfur (16): 2, 8, 6. Chlorine (17): 2, 8, 7. Argon (18): 2, 8, 8. Potassium (19): 2, 8, 8, 1. Calcium (20): 2, 8, 8, 2.

Linking Electronic Configuration to Position

The electronic configuration of an element tells you exactly where it sits in the periodic table. Look at sodium (2, 8, 1): the outer shell has 1 electron, so sodium is in Group 1; there are 3 occupied shells, so sodium is in Period 3. This pattern holds for every element in the first 20.

This link also works in reverse — if you know an element is in Group 6, Period 3, you can immediately write its electronic configuration: 2, 8, 6 (which is sulfur, atomic number 16). The exam often asks you to deduce the group and period from a configuration, or to predict a configuration from a position.

Key Fact

Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, which is why they react in similar ways. For example, all Group 1 metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) have one outer electron and react by losing it to form a +1 ion.

Metals and Non-Metals

The periodic table is divided into metals and non-metals. Metals are found on the left-hand side and in the centre of the table; non-metals sit on the right. The dividing line runs in a rough staircase shape from boron down to astatine.

This division is linked to electronic configuration. Metals typically have 1, 2 or 3 electrons in their outer shell, which they can easily lose to form positive ions. Non-metals have 4 or more outer-shell electrons (or a full outer shell for the noble gases) and tend to gain or share electrons when they react.

Most metals are shiny solids at room temperature, have high melting points, high density, and conduct electricity well. Most non-metals have low boiling points and are poor conductors of electricity. There are exceptions — mercury is a liquid metal, and carbon (as graphite) conducts electricity despite being a non-metal — but these general trends hold for the majority of elements.

Trends Across a Period

Moving across a period from left to right, the number of outer-shell electrons increases by one for each element, while the number of shells stays the same. This means elements change from reactive metals on the left (Group 1), through less reactive metals, to non-metals, and finally to very unreactive noble gases on the right (Group 0).

In Period 3, for example, sodium (2, 8, 1) is a highly reactive metal, silicon (2, 8, 4) is a metalloid, chlorine (2, 8, 7) is a reactive non-metal, and argon (2, 8, 8) is an unreactive noble gas. The pattern is driven entirely by the electronic configuration.

Trends Down a Group

Moving down a group, each element has one more occupied electron shell than the element above it. The outer-shell electrons are further from the nucleus and are shielded by the inner shells. This affects how easily the element reacts. For metals (like Group 1), reactivity increases down the group because it becomes easier to lose the outer electron. For non-metals (like Group 7), reactivity decreases because it becomes harder to attract an extra electron into the outer shell.

Key Fact

Down a group, each element has more electron shells, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded. For Group 1 metals this makes it easier to lose the outer electron, so reactivity increases. For Group 7 non-metals, the greater distance makes it harder to gain an extra electron, so reactivity decreases.

The noble gases (helium, neon, argon) sit in Group 0 on the far right of the periodic table. They have full outer shells — helium has 2, neon has 2, 8, and argon has 2, 8, 8. Because their outer shells are already complete, noble gases are very stable and unreactive. They exist as single atoms (monatomic gases) and do not easily form bonds with other elements.

lessons.title: Ionic Bonding & Ionic Compounds
lessons.description: How ionic and covalent bonds form, dot-and-cross diagrams, and the properties they produce.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Ionic Bonding?

When metals react with non-metals, atoms transfer electrons from one to the other. The metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positively charged ion called a cation. The non-metal atom gains those electrons and becomes a negatively charged ion called an anion. The strong electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions is an ionic bond.

An ion is simply an atom (or group of atoms) that has gained or lost electrons, giving it a net charge. In a neutral atom the number of protons equals the number of electrons. Once electrons are transferred, this balance is broken and the particle carries a charge.

Key Fact

Ionic bonds form by the transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. The metal loses electrons to form a positive ion (cation); the non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion (anion). Both ions end up with a full outer shell of electrons, giving them a stable electronic configuration.

Ion Formation — Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7

You need to predict which ions elements form based on their position in the periodic table. The Edexcel specification limits ionic compound formation to elements in Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7:

Group 1 elements (e.g. sodium, potassium) lose 1 electron to form ions with a +1 charge — for example, \(\text{Na}^+\) and \(\text{K}^+\). Group 2 elements (e.g. magnesium, calcium) lose 2 electrons to form ions with a +2 charge — for example, \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\).

Group 7 elements (e.g. chlorine, bromine) gain 1 electron to form ions with a −1 charge — for example, \(\text{Cl}^-\) and \(\text{Br}^-\). Group 6 elements (e.g. oxygen, sulfur) gain 2 electrons to form ions with a −2 charge — for example, \(\text{O}^{2-}\) and \(\text{S}^{2-}\).

Dot-and-cross diagrams show how electrons are transferred during ionic bonding. The electrons from the metal atom are drawn as crosses and the non-metal’s electrons as dots (or vice versa). After transfer, you draw square brackets around each ion and write its charge. For sodium chloride: sodium (2, 8, 1) loses its outer electron (shown as a cross) to chlorine (2, 8, 7), which gains it. Both ions achieve a full outer shell — \(\text{Na}^+\) (2, 8) and \(\text{Cl}^-\) (2, 8, 8).

For magnesium oxide: magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses two outer electrons, both transferring to oxygen (2, 6), giving \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) (2, 8) and \(\text{O}^{2-}\) (2, 8).

Calculating Protons, Neutrons and Electrons in Ions

When an atom forms an ion, the number of protons stays the same but the number of electrons changes. A sodium atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons. When it forms \(\text{Na}^+\), it still has 11 protons but only 10 electrons. A chlorine atom has 17 protons and 17 electrons; as \(\text{Cl}^-\) it has 17 protons and 18 electrons.

To find the electrons in any simple ion: start with the atomic number (number of electrons in a neutral atom), then subtract the charge for positive ions or add the charge for negative ions.

Naming Ionic Compounds

Ionic compounds are named using specific rules. When a compound contains just two elements, its name ends in –ide. For example, sodium and chlorine form sodium chloride; magnesium and oxygen form magnesium oxide. When a compound contains a metal, a non-metal and oxygen, its name typically ends in –ate. For example, copper sulfate contains copper, sulfur and oxygen; calcium carbonate contains calcium, carbon and oxygen.

Key Fact

Names ending in –ide tell you the compound contains only two elements (e.g. sodium chloride = sodium + chlorine). Names ending in –ate tell you the compound also contains oxygen (e.g. sodium sulfate = sodium + sulfur + oxygen).

Deducing Formulae of Ionic Compounds

To work out the formula of an ionic compound, you need to balance the charges so they cancel out to zero. For sodium chloride: \(\text{Na}^+\) has a +1 charge and \(\text{Cl}^-\) has a −1 charge, so one of each gives NaCl. For magnesium chloride: \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) needs two \(\text{Cl}^-\) ions to balance, giving \(\text{MgCl}_2\).

Positive ions: \(\text{Na}^+\), \(\text{K}^+\), \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\). Negative ions: chloride \(\text{Cl}^-\), bromide \(\text{Br}^-\), oxide \(\text{O}^{2-}\), sulfide \(\text{S}^{2-}\), hydroxide \(\text{OH}^-\), nitrate \(\text{NO}_3^-\), carbonate \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\), sulfate \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\). To deduce a formula, balance the total positive charge against the total negative charge so they sum to zero.

The Ionic Lattice

Ionic compounds do not exist as individual pairs of ions. Instead, billions of ions arrange themselves into a regular, repeating three-dimensional structure called a lattice. Each positive ion is surrounded by negative ions, and each negative ion is surrounded by positive ions. The strong electrostatic forces of attraction between these oppositely charged ions act in all directions throughout the lattice, holding the structure firmly together.

Key Fact

Ionic compounds form giant lattice structures. The strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions require a large amount of energy to overcome, which is why ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.

Properties of Ionic Compounds

Ionic compounds share several distinctive properties, all explained by their lattice structure:

High melting and boiling points — the strong ionic bonds throughout the lattice need a lot of energy to break. Conductivity when solid — ionic compounds do not conduct electricity as solids because the ions are locked in fixed positions and cannot move. Conductivity when molten or dissolved — when melted or dissolved in water, the ions become free to move and can carry an electrical current, so the compound conducts.

When an ionic compound dissolves in water, the lattice breaks apart and the individual ions become surrounded by water molecules. These free ions can now move through the solution towards electrodes. Positive ions (cations) move to the negative electrode and negative ions (anions) move to the positive electrode, carrying the charge and completing the circuit. This is why ionic compounds only conduct when molten or in solution — never as a solid.

lessons.title: Covalent Bonding & Molecular Structures
lessons.description: Covalent bonding, molecular structures, properties of simple molecular substances, giant covalent structures, and metallic bonding.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Covalent Bonding?

When two non-metal atoms react, neither atom is strong enough to take electrons from the other. Instead, the atoms share one or more pairs of electrons so that both achieve a full outer shell. This shared pair of electrons is a covalent bond. Covalent bonding produces molecules — distinct groups of atoms bonded together.

A typical atom has a radius of about \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m, while a small molecule such as water is roughly the same order of magnitude in size. You can represent covalent bonds using dot-and-cross diagrams, which show clearly which electrons belong to which atom and how they are shared.

Key Fact

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair. The atoms are held together because the shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei.

Simple Molecular Substances

You need to be able to draw dot-and-cross diagrams for six key molecules:

Hydrogen (\(\text{H}_2\)) — each hydrogen atom has 1 electron. They share one pair, forming a single bond. Hydrogen chloride (HCl) — hydrogen shares its 1 electron with one of chlorine’s 7 outer electrons, forming a single bond. Water (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\)) — oxygen has 6 outer electrons and shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms, forming two single bonds.

Methane (\(\text{CH}_4\)) — carbon has 4 outer electrons and shares one pair with each of four hydrogen atoms, forming four single bonds. Oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)) — each oxygen atom has 6 outer electrons. They share two pairs of electrons, forming a double bond. Carbon dioxide (\(\text{CO}_2\)) — each oxygen shares two pairs of electrons with the central carbon atom, forming two double bonds.

Step 1: Write the electronic configuration of each atom. Step 2: Identify how many electrons each atom needs to share to fill its outer shell. Step 3: Draw the outer shells overlapping, with shared electrons in the overlap region. Use dots for one atom’s electrons and crosses for the other. Step 4: Check that each atom has a full outer shell (2 for hydrogen, 8 for most other atoms).

For example, in water: oxygen (2, 6) needs 2 more electrons, hydrogen (1) needs 1 more. Two hydrogen atoms each share one electron with oxygen, giving oxygen 8 outer electrons and each hydrogen 2.

Properties of Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points. This is because the covalent bonds within each molecule are strong, but the forces between molecules — called intermolecular forces — are very weak. When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, it is these weak intermolecular forces that are overcome, not the covalent bonds themselves.

Simple molecular substances also do not conduct electricity because they have no free electrons or ions to carry a charge. Examples include water, methane, carbon dioxide and oxygen.

Key Fact

When a simple molecular substance boils, it is the weak intermolecular forces between molecules that are overcome — not the strong covalent bonds within the molecules. This is why simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points.

Giant Covalent Structures

Some covalent substances do not form small molecules. Instead, billions of atoms are bonded together in a continuous three-dimensional network called a giant covalent structure. These have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken to separate the atoms.

Diamond and Graphite

Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon — they are allotropes. In diamond, each carbon atom bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral arrangement. There are no free electrons, so diamond does not conduct electricity. Its hardness makes it ideal for cutting tools.

In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to only three others, forming flat layers. The fourth outer electron on each carbon atom is delocalised — free to move between the layers. These delocalised electrons allow graphite to conduct electricity, which is why graphite is used to make electrodes. The layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces, so they can slide over each other, making graphite soft and useful as a lubricant.

Fullerenes are carbon molecules formed into hollow shapes. The most famous is buckminsterfullerene, \(\text{C}_{60}\), which has 60 carbon atoms arranged in a sphere of hexagons and pentagons, resembling a football. Fullerenes can be used to deliver drugs to specific cells in the body and as catalysts.

Graphene is a single layer of graphite — just one atom thick. Each carbon atom is bonded to three others in a hexagonal pattern, with one delocalised electron per atom. Graphene is extremely strong, lightweight, and an excellent conductor of both electricity and heat. It has potential applications in electronics, composites and touchscreens.

Polymers

A polymer is a very long chain molecule made by joining together thousands of small molecules called monomers. For example, poly(ethene) is formed when many ethene molecules join together. The polymer chain consists of a long backbone of carbon atoms with hydrogen atoms attached. Polymers are simple molecular in the sense that their molecules — although very large — are held to each other by weak intermolecular forces.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, atoms are packed closely together in a regular arrangement. The outer electrons become delocalised — they are free to move throughout the entire structure. This creates a “sea” of delocalised electrons surrounding a lattice of positive metal ions. The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is a metallic bond.

Metallic bonding explains why metals are good conductors of electricity — the delocalised electrons can flow through the structure when a voltage is applied. Metals are also malleable because the layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonds, since the electron sea simply adjusts around them.

Key Fact

Metals conduct electricity because delocalised electrons can flow through the structure. Metals are malleable because the layers of ions can slide past each other without the bonding breaking down.

Dot-and-cross diagrams, ball-and-stick models, and 2D/3D representations are all useful for understanding bonding, but each has limitations. Dot-and-cross diagrams show electron arrangement clearly but not the 3D shape of a molecule. Ball-and-stick models show 3D shape but not electron distribution. 2D diagrams cannot fully represent 3D structures like diamond or giant ionic lattices. It is important to recognise that models are simplifications — they help us understand aspects of reality, but no single model captures everything.

lessons.title: Metallic Bonding & Properties of Materials
lessons.description: Metallic bonding, the structure of metals, properties explained by the metallic bonding model, and comparisons between different types of chemical bonding.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Metallic Bonding?

Metals have a distinctive type of bonding that is different from both ionic and covalent bonding. In a metal, the atoms are arranged in a regular pattern called a lattice. The outer-shell electrons of each metal atom are delocalised — they are no longer attached to any particular atom and are free to move throughout the whole structure.

This creates a structure of positive metal ions (cations) surrounded by a “sea” of delocalised electrons. The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and the negatively charged delocalised electrons holds the structure together. This attraction is what we call a metallic bond.

Key Fact

Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons. The metal ions are arranged in a regular lattice structure.

Properties of Metals

The metallic bonding model explains several key properties of metals. Most metals are shiny solids at room temperature with high melting and boiling points. This is because a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic attraction between the metal ions and the delocalised electrons.

Metals are good conductors of electricity because their delocalised electrons can move freely through the lattice, carrying electrical charge. They are also good conductors of heat because the delocalised electrons transfer kinetic energy rapidly through the structure.

Metals are malleable (can be hammered into shape) and ductile (can be drawn into wires). When a force is applied to a metal, the layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bonds, because the delocalised electrons can shift position to maintain the attraction. This is different from ionic compounds, which shatter when layers shift because ions of the same charge are forced next to each other.

Key Fact

Metals have high melting points (strong bonds), conduct electricity (delocalised electrons carry charge), and are malleable (layers slide without breaking bonds). All three properties are explained by the sea of delocalised electrons.

Most non-metals have low boiling points and are poor conductors of electricity. This is because non-metals form covalent bonds rather than metallic bonds. In simple molecular substances, the molecules are held together by weak intermolecular forces, which require little energy to overcome. There are no delocalised electrons, so they cannot conduct electricity.

Comparing Types of Substance

In the exam, you may need to compare the properties of ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent, and metallic substances. Each type of structure has distinctive physical properties that link directly to its bonding and structure.

Ionic compounds (e.g. sodium chloride) have high melting points because of strong electrostatic forces between ions. They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water because the ions are free to move, but not when solid because ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice.

Simple molecular substances (e.g. water, methane) have low melting and boiling points because the intermolecular forces between molecules are weak. They do not conduct electricity because they have no free charged particles.

Giant covalent substances (e.g. diamond, graphite) have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Diamond does not conduct electricity because all electrons are involved in bonding. Graphite is unusual — it conducts electricity because each carbon atom forms only three covalent bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can carry charge.

Diamond has each carbon atom bonded to four others in a rigid tetrahedral structure. This makes diamond extremely hard, which is why it is used in cutting tools. Graphite has carbon atoms arranged in layers of hexagons. The weak forces between the layers allow them to slide over each other, making graphite useful as a lubricant and in pencils. Fullerenes such as \(C_{60}\) (buckminsterfullerene) are hollow carbon molecules and carbon nanotubes are tiny cylinders of carbon atoms, both with potential uses in electronics, drug delivery, and as catalysts.

Polymers

Polymers such as poly(ethene) are large molecules consisting of long chains of carbon atoms. Because polymer molecules are large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong, giving polymers higher melting points than simple molecular substances. However, they do not conduct electricity because there are no free electrons or ions.

Key Fact

The four types of substance — ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent, and metallic — can be distinguished by their melting points, solubility in water, and ability to conduct electricity. These properties are explained by the type of bonding and structure present.

lessons.title: Conservation of Mass & Moles
lessons.description: The law of conservation of mass, relative formula mass, balancing equations, moles, empirical and molecular formulae, and limiting reactants.
lessons.content_html:
The Law of Conservation of Mass

In any chemical reaction, no atoms are created or destroyed — they are simply rearranged to form new substances. This means that the total mass of the reactants always equals the total mass of the products. This principle is known as the law of conservation of mass.

If you carry out a reaction in a sealed (closed) container — for example, a precipitation reaction in a stoppered flask — the mass before and after the reaction will be identical. This is because nothing can enter or leave the system.

Key Fact

In an open container, mass may appear to change. If a gas is produced (e.g. \(CO_2\) from a carbonate reacting with acid), the gas escapes and the mass decreases. If a gas is taken in (e.g. when magnesium burns in air and gains oxygen), the mass of the solid product increases. In both cases, mass is actually conserved — but some of it has entered or left the container.

Relative Formula Mass

The relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of a compound is found by adding up the relative atomic masses (\(A_r\)) of every atom in its formula. For example, for water (\(H_2O\)):

$$M_r = (2 \times 1) + 16 = 18$$

For calcium carbonate (\(CaCO_3\)):

$$M_r = 40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 100$$

You can calculate the percentage by mass of an element in a compound using:

$$\text{percentage by mass} = \frac{A_r \times \text{number of atoms of element}}{M_r} \times 100$$

For example, the percentage by mass of oxygen in water (\(H_2O\), \(M_r = 18\)):

$$\frac{16}{18} \times 100 = 88.9\%$$

Balancing Equations and Reacting Masses

A balanced chemical equation shows the same number of atoms of each element on both sides. This reflects the law of conservation of mass. You can use a balanced equation to calculate the mass of reactants or products.

Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 10 g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid:

$$CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2$$

Step 1: Find the \(M_r\) of \(CaCO_3 = 100\) and \(CO_2 = 44\).

Step 2: From the equation, 1 mole of \(CaCO_3\) produces 1 mole of \(CO_2\), so 100 g of \(CaCO_3\) produces 44 g of \(CO_2\).

Step 3: Scale down: \(\frac{10}{100} \times 44 = 4.4\) g of \(CO_2\).

Key Fact

To calculate reacting masses: (1) write the balanced equation, (2) find the \(M_r\) of the substances involved, (3) use the mole ratio from the equation to scale up or down from the known mass.

The Mole

The mole is a unit used to measure the amount of a substance. One mole of any substance contains exactly \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\) particles (atoms, molecules, or ions). This number is called the Avogadro constant.

The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass. For example, one mole of carbon (\(A_r = 12\)) has a mass of 12 g. One mole of water (\(M_r = 18\)) has a mass of 18 g.

The key equation linking mass and moles is:

$$\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass (g)}}{M_r}$$

Key Fact

One mole of any substance contains \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\) particles (the Avogadro constant). To convert between mass and moles, use: moles = mass \(\div\) \(M_r\).

The concentration of a solution tells you how much solute is dissolved in a given volume. It is calculated using:

$$\text{concentration (g/dm}^3\text{)} = \frac{\text{mass of solute (g)}}{\text{volume of solution (dm}^3\text{)}}$$

For example, if 5 g of sodium chloride is dissolved in 250 cm\(^3\) of water (= 0.25 dm\(^3\)):

$$\text{concentration} = \frac{5}{0.25} = 20 \text{ g/dm}^3$$

Empirical and Molecular Formulae

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. It can be calculated from reacting masses or percentage composition. The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms in one molecule and can be deduced from the empirical formula and the relative molecular mass.

For example, ethane has the molecular formula \(C_2H_6\). Its empirical formula is \(CH_3\) (dividing by the common factor of 2).

You can determine the empirical formula of magnesium oxide by heating a known mass of magnesium ribbon in a crucible. Weigh the crucible before and after heating. The increase in mass equals the mass of oxygen that reacted. Divide each mass by its \(A_r\) to find the mole ratio, then simplify to get the empirical formula (MgO).

Limiting Reactants

In most reactions, one reactant is used up before the other. The reactant that is completely used up is called the limiting reactant — it controls the amount of product formed. The other reactant is said to be in excess. Adding more of the excess reactant will not produce any more product.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases & Making Salts
lessons.description: Properties of acids and alkalis, pH indicators, strong and weak acids, bases, neutralisation reactions, and salt preparation methods.
lessons.content_html:
Acids and Alkalis

An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when dissolved in water. An alkali is a soluble base that produces hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)) when dissolved in water. The pH scale runs from 0 (strongly acidic) through 7 (neutral) to 14 (strongly alkaline).

Common indicators help identify whether a solution is acidic, neutral, or alkaline. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in alkali. Methyl orange turns red in acid and yellow in alkali. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali.

Key Fact

Acids produce \(H^+\) ions in solution. Alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions in solution. A neutral solution has pH 7. Below pH 7 is acidic; above pH 7 is alkaline.

Strong and Weak Acids

A strong acid is one that completely dissociates (breaks apart) into ions in water. Examples include hydrochloric acid (\(HCl\)), sulfuric acid (\(H_2SO_4\)), and nitric acid (\(HNO_3\)). A weak acid only partially dissociates — most of its molecules remain intact. Examples include ethanoic acid and citric acid.

The terms dilute and concentrated refer to how much acid is dissolved in a given volume of water. A dilute solution has a small amount of acid per unit volume; a concentrated solution has a large amount. The terms dilute/concentrated are about how much solute is present, while strong/weak are about how much the acid ionises.

The higher the concentration of \(H^+\) ions, the lower the pH. As the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10, the pH decreases by 1.

Bases and Neutralisation

A base is any substance that reacts with an acid to produce a salt and water only. Alkalis are bases that dissolve in water. Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base.

The ionic equation for an acid–alkali neutralisation is:

$$H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$$

Acids react with different types of bases to produce salts:

Acid + metal \(\rightarrow\) salt + hydrogen (e.g. \(Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2\))

Acid + metal oxide \(\rightarrow\) salt + water (e.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\))

Acid + metal hydroxide \(\rightarrow\) salt + water (e.g. \(NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\))

Acid + metal carbonate \(\rightarrow\) salt + water + carbon dioxide (e.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\))

Key Fact

The name of the salt produced depends on the acid used: hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates, and nitric acid makes nitrates. The metal in the salt comes from the base.

Hydrogen is tested using a burning splint — it burns with a squeaky pop. Carbon dioxide is tested by bubbling it through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) — the limewater turns milky (cloudy).

Making Soluble Salts

Soluble salts can be made in two ways, depending on whether the base is soluble or insoluble.

Method 1: Using an insoluble base (e.g. metal oxide, carbonate). Add excess insoluble base to the acid. The excess base ensures all the acid has reacted. Filter off the excess solid. Evaporate the remaining solution (or leave to crystallise) to obtain the salt crystals.

Method 2: Using a soluble base (alkali). A titration must be used. Measure the acid into a flask using a pipette, add a few drops of indicator, then add the alkali from a burette until the indicator shows neutralisation. Mix the acid and alkali in exactly the right proportions (without indicator this time), then evaporate to obtain salt crystals.

To prepare pure, dry hydrated copper sulfate crystals: (1) Warm dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker. (2) Add excess copper oxide powder and stir until no more dissolves. (3) Filter off the excess copper oxide. (4) Pour the blue copper sulfate solution into an evaporating basin. (5) Heat gently on a water bath until crystals start to form, then leave to cool and crystallise. (6) Pat dry with filter paper.

Solubility Rules and Precipitates

Solubility rules help you predict whether a salt is soluble or insoluble in water:

All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble. All nitrates are soluble. Most chlorides are soluble (except silver chloride and lead chloride). Most sulfates are soluble (except lead sulfate, barium sulfate and calcium sulfate). Most carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble (except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium).

When two solutions are mixed, if the ions can form an insoluble compound, a precipitate forms. For example, mixing silver nitrate solution with sodium chloride solution produces an insoluble white precipitate of silver chloride.

Key Fact

An insoluble salt can be made by mixing two solutions that contain the required ions. The precipitate is filtered off, washed with distilled water, and dried.

lessons.title: Electrolysis & Extraction of Metals
lessons.description: Electrolysis of ionic compounds, extraction of metals from ores, half equations, oxidation-reduction, and the reactivity series.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using electrical energy from a direct current (d.c.) supply to decompose (break down) an ionic compound. The ionic compound must be either molten or dissolved in water so that its ions are free to move. In this state, the compound is called an electrolyte.

During electrolysis, two electrodes are placed in the electrolyte and connected to a d.c. power supply. Positively charged ions (cations) are attracted to the negatively charged electrode (the cathode). Negatively charged ions (anions) are attracted to the positively charged electrode (the anode).

Key Fact

Cations (positive ions) migrate to the cathode (negative electrode). Anions (negative ions) migrate to the anode (positive electrode). Remember: Positive And Negative = PAN — Positive goes to the Anode? No! Positive goes to Negative (cathode).

Electrolysis of Specific Substances

When electrolysing molten ionic compounds (e.g. molten lead bromide), the products are straightforward: the metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal forms at the anode. Lead bromide gives lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode.

Electrolysis of solutions is more complex because water also contains ions (\(H^+\) and \(OH^-\)). The product at each electrode depends on the position of the element in the reactivity series:

At the cathode: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is deposited.

At the anode: If a halide ion is present, the halogen is produced. If no halide is present, oxygen is produced from the water.

Copper chloride solution: Copper at the cathode (Cu is less reactive than H), chlorine at the anode (halide present). Sodium chloride solution: Hydrogen at the cathode (Na is more reactive than H), chlorine at the anode (halide present). Sodium sulfate solution: Hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode (no halide). Acidified water (dilute sulfuric acid): Hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode.

Half Equations & Oxidation-Reduction

Oxidation is the loss of electrons. Reduction is the gain of electrons. Remember OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

At the cathode, reduction occurs — cations gain electrons. At the anode, oxidation occurs — anions lose electrons. Half equations show what happens at each electrode separately:

For molten lead bromide:

Cathode (reduction): \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\)

Anode (oxidation): \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\)

Key Fact

Reduction always occurs at the cathode (cations gain electrons). Oxidation always occurs at the anode (anions lose electrons). OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

When copper sulfate solution is electrolysed using copper electrodes (not inert), the copper anode dissolves and pure copper is deposited on the cathode. This is used industrially to purify copper. The impure copper is the anode, the pure copper is the cathode, and the electrolyte is copper sulfate solution. The anode loses mass and the cathode gains mass.

Cathode: \(Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu\). Anode: \(Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-\).

The Reactivity Series

Metals can be ranked by their reactivity with water, dilute acids, and salt solutions. The reactivity series (most to least reactive) is: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold. More reactive metals react more vigorously with water and acids, and have a greater tendency to form positive ions (cations).

In a displacement reaction, a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. For example, iron displaces copper from copper sulfate solution because iron is more reactive than copper:

$$Fe + CuSO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu$$

Extracting Metals from Ores

Most metals are found in the Earth’s crust as ores — compounds that must be chemically processed to obtain the pure metal. Unreactive metals such as gold are found as uncombined elements because they do not readily react with other substances.

Extracting a metal from its ore involves reduction — removing the oxygen. The method of extraction depends on the metal’s position in the reactivity series:

Metals below carbon (e.g. iron, zinc, copper) can be extracted by heating the ore with carbon. Carbon is more reactive, so it displaces the metal. For example: \(2Fe_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Fe + 3CO_2\).

Metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium, sodium) are too reactive to be extracted by carbon. They must be extracted by electrolysis of the molten ore, which is more expensive because it requires large amounts of electrical energy.

Key Fact

Metals less reactive than carbon are extracted by heating with carbon (reduction). Metals more reactive than carbon must be extracted by electrolysis. Electrolysis is more expensive due to the energy costs.

Recycling metals saves energy (less mining and extraction needed), preserves finite ore reserves, and reduces landfill. A life-cycle assessment evaluates the environmental impact of a product from obtaining raw materials through manufacturing, use, and disposal. These assessments help compare the true environmental cost of products and materials.

Bioleaching uses bacteria to extract metals from low-grade ores. The bacteria produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds. Phytoextraction uses plants that absorb metal ions from the soil through their roots. The plants are then harvested and burned, and the metal is extracted from the ash. Both methods are slower than traditional mining but are less environmentally damaging and can be used on ores with very low metal concentrations.
